name: Napoleon Blue
lede: Napoleon Blue is a deep, violet-leaning blue that Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates to 1850, nearly thirty years after the emperor it is named for died.

sections.title: A name outliving its namesake
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul place this value at plate 44, position C 11, first recorded in 1850 [1]. The dictionary's own records show the same plate position carrying another name, Bleu de Lyon, from 1928, almost eighty years later, which our library notes without saying which name came first in actual use [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies it as a deep blue, about 5.4 units from that block's reference chip [2]. Napoleon Bonaparte died in 1821, so the color word postdates him by about three decades; whether it alludes to a uniform, a flag or simply the emperor's name as a byword for grandeur is not stated in the sources consulted [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[navy|Navy]], and it sits near [[newport|Newport]], [[berlin-blue|Berlin Blue]] and [[cornflower|Cornflower]] on the same deep-blue stretch of the chart [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Napoleon Blue covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 32 works, as photographed [3]. It is strongly tied to two painters relative to their output, Vilhelm Lundstrøm and Henri Matisse, and it peaks in paintings from the 1900s decade, over four times expected [3]. It functions mostly as a shadow color and keeps company almost entirely with Navy [3]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished canvases read as screen colors, not pigment tests [3].
